text: Nowadays, employees often can autonomously change, adapt, modify and tailor their jobs or the way in which they perform their jobs ( Parker, 2000 ; Organ et al., 2006 ; Oldham and Hackman, 2010 ). The question as to what determines how individuals customize their jobs, and ultimately their careers, has received increasing research attention ( Parker and Bindl, 2017 ). Several scholars have argued that how a person’s career unfolds is strongly affected by his or her own values, personality characteristics, goals and preferences ( Hall, 2004 ; Wille et al., 2012 ; Savickas, 2013 ). The Big Five trait taxonomy ( McCrae and Costa, 1996 , 1999 ; also see the Five Factor Model [FFM], Goldberg, 1990 ) appears to offer a particularly promising approach to the application of personality constructs to career related outcomes. Indeed, the Big Five is an empirically validated classification of the structure and nature of personality traits. Its usefulness for predicting job crafting behavior and career role enactment is apparent from several studies that show personality traits do indeed affect the way in which people perform their jobs over time ( Wille et al., 2010 , 2012 ; Bakker et al., 2012 ).
